pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Investigating Forces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** UK KS3 national curriculum ('forces measured in newtons, measurements of stretch or compression as force is changed; force-extension linear relation; Hooke's Law as a special case').

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NGSS MS-PS2-2 Science-and-Engineering Practice ('Plan an investigation... identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim');

- **Operational details:** This is a working-scientifically (procedural) topic at 12-13: pupils plan and carry out force investigations — measuring force with a newton meter, investigating Hooke's Law (force vs extension), and collecting motion data to test Newton's laws. The procedural core is variable control (independent = force applied, dependent = extension, control = the spring), accurate measurement, and turning data into a force–extension graph with a line of best fit.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational/quantitative). At KS3 this stops short of the spring-constant equation (F = ke) and gradient calculation — those are GCSE; the focus is the proportional relationship (straight line through the origin), the limit of proportionality where it bends, careful measurement, and the graphing skill itself.
bestPractices: Control variables explicitly: IV = force applied, DV = extension, CV = the spring; change one variable at a time (NGSS SEP; KS3 working scientifically)
Use a newton meter correctly (it reads force directly in N), or convert masses to weight via W=m×g; measure EXTENSION (the increase in length), not the total length
Add force in equal steps, let the spring settle, record carefully, and repeat on unloading; read the ruler squarely using a set square to improve accuracy (Oak)
Plot Force (y) against Extension (x), draw a line of best fit, and identify the directly proportional region (straight line through the origin) and the limit of proportionality where it bends
Hold the KS3 ceiling: do not require F = ke or spring-constant gradient (that is GCSE) — focus on the proportional relationship, graphing and measurement craft
For the Newton's-laws strand, calculate acceleration from measured force and mass and compare with the trolley's actual motion (testing F=ma); include a risk assessment for hanging masses
keyRepresentations: Clamped spring + ruler + slotted masses (or newton meter) apparatus set-up
Force–extension graph with a line of best fit through the origin and a marked limit of proportionality
Variable-control planning frame (IV/DV/CV) and a results table with load-and-unload repeat readings
commonMisconceptions: The line of best fit must pass through every data point (Oak-named graphing misconception) — antidote: have pupils invent plots with small measurement errors so the line is seen to average scatter
Measuring the spring's total length instead of its extension
Recording force in grams/kilograms rather than newtons; treating mass as if it were a force
Changing more than one variable, or not repeating readings
Assuming proportionality continues forever — ignoring the limit of proportionality
Describing the pattern as 'the length doubles per newton' rather than 'the same extension is added per newton'

learn.summary: For pupils aged 12–13, this is a working-scientifically (procedural) goal: plan and carry out force investigations — measuring force with a newton meter, investigating the force–extension relationship (Hooke's Law), and collecting motion data to test Newton's Second Law. The craft to be learned is variable control (independent = force applied, dependent = extension, control = the same spring), accurate measurement of EXTENSION (increase in length, not total length), repeating readings, and turning real, scattered data into a force–extension graph with a line of best fit. At this level, stop short of the spring-constant equation (F = ke) and gradient calculation (those are later GCSE content); focus on the proportional relationship (a straight line through the origin), the limit of proportionality where it bends, and careful measurement and graphing. The strongest learning combines a hands-on practical with real apparatus and a graph-building task that confronts the best-fit misconception as scatter appears.

activities.title: Hooke's Law practical with real apparatus
feedback: If a learner plots or records the spring's total length, prompt: extension = current length − natural length; the natural length must be measured and subtracted first.
If force is recorded in grams or kilograms, remind that those are masses; weight (a force) in newtons is W = m × g, or read force directly from the newton meter.
If only one reading is taken per load, prompt a repeat and a mean at each step so anomalies can be judged — this is a scaffold, not a reteach of the whole method.
If more than one variable changes, point back to the IV/DV/CV plan: keep the same spring and change only the force.
activities.rationale: The learning target is measurement craft with physical apparatus — handling equipment, reading instruments squarely, measuring extension, and coping with genuine scatter — which is developed through hands-on practice rather than recognition tasks alone.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-2 SEP (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, 6-8): plan an investigation individually and collaboratively and in the design identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to gather data, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim.

KS3 statutory content: 'forces measured in newtons, measurements of stretch or compression as force is changed; force-extension linear relation; Hooke's Law as a special case'; deformation forces associated with stretching/squashing springs.

KS3 Hooke's law practical: extension is directly proportional to force (straight line through origin), measure extension not length, IV=force/DV=extension/CV=spring, draw a line of best fit (it need not pass through every point), identify the limit of proportionality; KS3 does not require F=ke or the spring-constant gradient.
learnerActions: Clamp a spring, measure and record its natural (unstretched) length first.
State the variables before starting: independent = force applied (added in equal steps), dependent = extension, control = the same spring throughout.
Add weight one equal step at a time (hang slotted masses and convert to weight using W = m × g, or read force directly in newtons from a newton meter), letting the spring settle each time.
Measure the new length at each load and read the ruler squarely — line your eye level with the mark, or use a set square against the ruler to avoid parallax error.
Calculate extension at each step: extension = current length − natural length.
Repeat each reading (and read again on unloading) and take a mean, so scatter and anomalies become visible.
Record force in newtons and extension in a results table.
activities.intendedInsight: Force is measured in newtons; extension (not total length) is the quantity that responds to force; controlling variables and repeating readings is what makes the relationship trustworthy.

activities.title: Plotting force vs extension and drawing a line of best fit
feedback: If a learner connects the points to make a kinked line, explain that real readings scatter: draw ONE best-fit straight line with points either side so anomalies stand out.
If the line does not pass through the origin and the learner doesn't notice, check whether total length was plotted instead of extension.

If a learner extrapolates the straight line indefinitely or forces a straight line through the curved high-load points, prompt them to load past the limit so they can SEE the curve and mark where proportionality ends.
Encourage the phrasing 'the same extension is added per newton' rather than 'the length doubles per newton'.
activities.rationale: The best-fit-through-every-point error and the 'proportional forever' error are the key graphing and conceptual misconceptions here; confronting real scatter and the bending line directly addresses both, while keeping the limit of proportionality distinct from the elastic limit.
sourceClaims: KS3 Hooke's law practical: extension is directly proportional to force (straight line through origin), measure extension not length, IV=force/DV=extension/CV=spring, draw a line of best fit (it need not pass through every point), identify the limit of proportionality; KS3 does not require F=ke or the spring-constant gradient.
learnerActions: Plot Force (newtons) on the y-axis against Extension on the x-axis using your recorded data.
Draw a single straight line of best fit through the scattered points — do NOT join the dots point-to-point; aim for a line with roughly equal numbers of points on each side.

Describe the pattern in words: up to the limit of proportionality, equal steps of force add the SAME extension each time (not 'the length doubles'), and with zero extension at zero force this means extension is directly proportional to force — a straight line through the origin.
Continue adding load in a second investigation (or extend the dataset) until the once-straight line starts to bend, and mark that point where proportionality ends — the limit of proportionality.

Separately, note that if the spring is loaded past its elastic limit (which for many springs is at or only a little beyond the limit of proportionality) it may be permanently stretched and no longer return to its natural length; this is a distinct idea from the limit of proportionality.
Explain why the line is drawn to average scatter rather than connecting every point.
activities.intendedInsight: A best-fit line averages real measurement scatter rather than connecting individual points; the force–extension relationship is proportional only up to a limit of proportionality, after which it bends (and, at still greater loads beyond the elastic limit, the spring may deform permanently).

activities.title: Testing Newton's Second Law with a trolley
feedback: If a learner expects perfect agreement, first check that m includes every mass being accelerated (trolley plus any hanging masses); then remind them that friction opposes the applied force, so the resultant (net) force is smaller than F and the observed acceleration is a little below the F/m prediction; measurement uncertainty adds further to the difference.

If a learner describes the force as setting the trolley's speed or current direction, remind them that the resultant force determines acceleration (change in motion), so the stated starting condition (e.g. from rest) matters when predicting how the motion changes.
activities.rationale: This strand connects measured force and mass to motion, extending the investigative method beyond springs and reinforcing variable control and quantitative reasoning.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-2 SEP (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, 6-8): plan an investigation individually and collaboratively and in the design identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to gather data, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim.
learnerActions: Apply a measured force to a trolley of known mass (include a risk assessment for any hanging masses).
State the trolley's starting condition (e.g. starting from rest) before describing how its motion changes.

Calculate the predicted acceleration using a = F / m, where F is the applied (driving) force and m is the total mass being accelerated (the trolley plus any hanging masses that move with it), assuming friction is small.
Measure the trolley's actual acceleration (e.g. with light gates or a motion sensor/data logger) and compare it with the calculated acceleration.
Discuss sources of difference (e.g. friction opposing the applied force, measurement error) between prediction and observation.
activities.intendedInsight: A measured applied force on a known total moving mass (trolley plus any hanging masses) predicts an acceleration via a = F/m when friction is small; more precisely, it is the resultant force (applied force minus friction) that determines acceleration — a change in motion, not an instant speed or direction. Because real friction makes the resultant smaller than the applied force, the observed acceleration is usually a little below F/m, and comparing prediction with real motion tests Newton's Second Law.

activities.title: Plan and reason about the method (companion check)
feedback: If a learner chooses the dot-to-dot line, re-explain that the best-fit line averages scatter.
If a learner mislabels the variables, point back to: force is changed (IV), extension responds (DV), the spring is kept the same (CV).
activities.rationale: These recognition and sequencing tasks assess the procedural reasoning behind the investigation; they can check planning and variable identification but do not themselves elicit the physical measurement, so they complement rather than replace running the investigation.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-2 SEP (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, 6-8): plan an investigation individually and collaboratively and in the design identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to gather data, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim.

KS3 Hooke's law practical: extension is directly proportional to force (straight line through origin), measure extension not length, IV=force/DV=extension/CV=spring, draw a line of best fit (it need not pass through every point), identify the limit of proportionality; KS3 does not require F=ke or the spring-constant gradient.
learnerActions: Put the method steps in the correct order: plan the variables, measure natural length, add load in equal steps, measure new length, calculate extension, repeat readings, plot, draw best-fit line, identify the limit of proportionality.
Identify which quantity is the independent variable, dependent variable, and control variable for the spring investigation.
Given a graph with scattered points, select or sketch the correct line of best fit (not the dot-to-dot line).
Given a force–extension graph that curves, mark the limit of proportionality.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure procedural reasoning — correct sequencing, variable identification, best-fit choice, and recognising the limit of proportionality — underpins a trustworthy investigation.

constraints: Keep to the KS3 ceiling: do not require the spring-constant equation (F = ke) or gradient calculation; focus on the proportional relationship, the limit of proportionality, graphing, and measurement craft.

The core learning is measurement craft with physical apparatus (reading a newton meter, measuring extension squarely, repeating readings, coping with genuine scatter). A screen-based graph-building task can rehearse the variable-control and best-fit logic and can make the scatter/limit visible as load is added, but it does not substitute for handling real apparatus — pair the two.

A live graph-building task (points dropping onto a force–extension plot as load is added, and a best-fit tool that deliberately does not snap through every point) is an optional way to make the best-fit and limit-of-proportionality ideas concrete. Marking where the line bends shows the limit of proportionality; a spring left permanently deformed is a separate, heavier-load effect (past the elastic limit). This is a useful illustration, not a mandatory mechanism.

Recognition and sequencing tasks (ordering steps, identifying IV/DV/CV, selecting the best-fit line, marking the limit) assess procedural reasoning but do not let learners run the investigation or collect real data; use them alongside, not instead of, practical work.
A labelled static apparatus diagram with a 'measure extension not length' and units callout is a helpful set-up and reference, but cannot build the graph or rehearse the best-fit decision.
Include a risk assessment for hanging masses in the Newton's Second Law trolley strand.

Always state the starting condition (e.g. from rest) when describing how a trolley's motion changes, since the resultant force determines acceleration (change in motion), not the current speed or direction of travel.

In the trolley strand, be explicit that F in a = F/m is the applied (driving) force used for the prediction, while the resultant (applied force minus friction) is what actually accelerates the trolley; do not label the predicting force as the resultant while also attributing the discrepancy to friction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (Oak National Academy KS3 Hooke's law lesson) is marked verified:false in the original row; treat its specific procedural claims as unconfirmed pending a source check.

The original recommendation conflates the limit of proportionality (where the line stops being straight) with the spring 'no longer springing back' (the elastic limit, a distinct heavier-load point). The rewrite separates these in the learner-facing activity and constraints; confirm the preferred KS3 terminology against the curriculum.

Audit note on the Newton's Second Law strand: the source says to 'compare a=F/m with the trolley's actual motion.' This is sound provided the trolley's initial state is specified and F is treated as the applied force when friction is small. The rewrite clarifies that the resultant force (applied minus friction) determines acceleration, which reconciles the friction-based discrepancy; whether the source intends F as applied or net force is not stated.
Self-audit: W = m × g (mass to weight) and extension = current length − natural length are stated correctly; no arithmetic errors found in the source values used.

probeDeeper: Why did you draw the line like that instead of joining each point?
What exactly did you plot on the y-axis — the length or the extension? Why does it matter?
How many times did you measure at each load, and what did you do with the repeats?
What would happen to your graph if you kept adding heavier and heavier masses?
assess.correctAnswer: Measures the spring's natural length, adds masses one at a time, records the force (weight of the masses, or from the newton meter) and the EXTENSION (new length minus natural length) at each step, repeating readings; plots force (or mass) against extension; draws a BEST-FIT straight line through the scattered points (not dot-to-dot), showing extension proportional to force; identifies the limit of proportionality where the line starts to curve. Controls variables (same spring, measures extension not total length).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Join the dots — draw the line through every single point.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain that real readings scatter; draw ONE best-fit straight line with points either side of it, so anomalies stand out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Connects the points dot-to-dot, producing a kinked line.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Plot the total LENGTH of the spring, not the extension.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extension = current length minus natural length; measure the unstretched length first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: y-values are full lengths; the line doesn't pass through the origin and the child doesn't notice.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The spring stretches in proportion no matter how much I add.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep loading past the limit of proportionality to SEE the curve; mark where proportionality ends.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Extrapolates the straight line indefinitely, or forces a straight line through curved high-load points.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'One reading per mass is enough — I won't repeat any.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt a repeat and a mean at each load — scaffold, don't reteach the method.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Takes single readings, so scatter and anomalies can't be judged.

responseLevels.gap: Records some readings but plots total length or dot-to-dots the points, takes single readings, or doesn't keep the spring the same — the relationship can't be read reliably.
responseLevels.full: Controls variables, measures extension with repeats, plots and draws a best-fit line showing extension proportional to force, and identifies the limit of proportionality where the line curves — using the newton meter correctly and treating scatter appropriately.
responseLevels.partial: Sets up the investigation, plots force vs extension and sees a rising line, but joins the dots, can't identify the limit of proportionality, or omits repeats — collecting data without the craft that makes the relationship (and its limit) trustworthy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a spring clamped at the top, a set of identical slotted masses, a ruler, and a newton meter. Investigate how the stretching force affects the spring's extension (Hooke's Law). Plan and carry out the investigation, record your results, plot a graph, and tell me what your graph shows about the relationship — including where, if anywhere, it stops being proportional.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch, don't ask. The load-bearing tells: (1) does the child plot EXTENSION (change in length) or mistakenly plot total length; (2) do they draw a best-fit line through real scatter, or connect every point dot-to-dot; (3) do they repeat readings and keep the spring the same; (4) do they recognise the limit of proportionality rather than forcing a straight line through curved data. Dot-to-dotting, plotting total length, or single readings show the procedure isn't secure even if numbers get recorded.
